blocks.html: For $H=H_0+H^\prime(t)$ with an exactly solvable $H_0$, move the trivial time evolution of $H_0$ from the states onto the operators. Both states and observables then depend on time: a compromise between the Schrödinger and the Heisenberg picture.
The state then evolves only under the perturbation, written in the Dirac picture:

Sit in a frame that rotates with $H_0$: if there were no perturbation, $\Psi_D$ would stand still. All motion you see is caused by $H^\prime$, which is why the expansion in powers of $H^\prime$ is natural.
Time ordering $T$ matters because $H^\prime_D(t)$ at different times need not commute. Only to first order can it be dropped.
The derivation of the first-order transition amplitude (next lesson) starts here: know (11.94) and the first-order term of (11.95).

enc.title: First-order time-dependent perturbation theory and Fermi's golden rule

blocks.html: Start in an eigenstate $|i\rangle$ of $H_0$ at $t_0$, ask for the probability to be found in $|f\rangle\perp|i\rangle$ later. To first order in $H^\prime$:
Sudden switch-on $H^\prime=V\theta(t)$:

Peak at $\omega_{if}=0$ of height $t^2/\hbar^2$ and width $\sim2\pi/t$: its area grows $\propto t$. Energy is conserved only up to $\Delta\omega_{if}\,t\sim2\pi$. Summing over a dense group of final states with density $\rho(E_f)$, $\sin^2(\omega t)/(\pi t\omega^2)\to\delta(\omega)$ gives a constant rate:
Short times: every final state is reachable (energy is fuzzy). Long times: only energy-conserving transitions accumulate, linearly in $t$, so the probability per unit time is constant.

Validity window: $t$ long enough that the peak $2\pi\hbar/t$ is narrower than the band $\Delta E_f$ over which $\langle f|V|i\rangle$ is constant, but short enough that many states $\delta\varepsilon$ lie under the peak (and $P\ll1$ so first order holds).
Older exams (HS14, HS16) ask for the golden rule directly: derive (11.100), explain the $t^2$ peak and its width, state $\Gamma$ with the conditions.

blocks.tex: H_Z=-\vec M\cdot\vec B,\qquad \vec M=\frac q{2mc}\vec L
blocks.label: script (9.45)-(9.47): orbital magnetic moment

blocks.html: The $\vec A^2$ term gives diamagnetism and is negligible for hydrogen in lab fields. For the electron ($q=-e$) the levels $(n,l,m)$ stay eigenstates, but the $m$-degeneracy is lifted:

A circulating charge is a current loop: magnetic moment $\propto$ angular momentum. $g\approx2$ for spin compensates the half-integer $s_z$: orbit and spin give the same splitting steps (script Abb. 18: a p level splits into a quintuplet).
Gaussian vs SI: the script writes $q/2mc$; in SI drop the $c$. And $\vec M$ is antiparallel to $\vec L$ for the electron because $q=-e$.
Typical: count the Zeeman lines of a level, derive $H_Z$ from minimal coupling, compare normal and anomalous Zeeman effect (FS26 Q4, sheet 14).

blocks.html: Alice and Bob share the singlet $|\psi\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt2}(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle)$ (particles 1, 2). Alice holds an unknown $|\varphi\rangle$ (particle 0) and may send only classical bits.
Alice measures particles 0 and 1 in the Bell basis:

Rewriting $|\varphi\rangle\otimes|\psi\rangle$ in this basis, each outcome $i$ (probability $\frac14$) leaves Bob’s particle in a fixed unitary image of $|\varphi\rangle$. Alice sends $i$ (2 bits), Bob applies:

The entanglement carries the “continuous” information, the two bits only tell Bob which of four rotations to undo. Nothing travels faster than light: without the bits Bob’s particle is maximally mixed.
No cloning: Alice’s measurement destroys $|\varphi\rangle$ on her side. And Alice never learns $|\varphi\rangle$.
Know the protocol, why 2 classical bits are needed, and why it does not allow superluminal signalling.

enc.title: Continuous spectra: the spectrum, the spectral theorem and probabilities

blocks.html: In infinite dimensions an observable need not have eigenvectors (a plane wave is not normalisable). The right generalisation is the spectrum:
Eigenvalues belong to $\sigma(A)$; for self-adjoint $A$ the spectrum is real, and it is the set of possible measurement results. Examples:

Spectral theorem: there is a unique map $f\mapsto f(A)$ with $f(A)=\sum_af(a)P_a$ in the discrete case. For an interval $I$, $P_I(A)$ (characteristic function) is an orthogonal projector, and $W_\psi(I)=\langle\psi|P_I(A)|\psi\rangle$ is the probability to measure a value in $I$, with $\langle A\rangle_\psi=\langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle$.

For a continuous spectrum you never get a sharp value with a normalisable state, only probabilities for intervals; $\|(A-\lambda)\psi\|\le\varepsilon$ says “almost eigenvectors” exist, e.g. very long wave packets for $p$.
$\delta$-normalised states like $|p\rangle$ are not elements of $\mathcal H$; they are a bookkeeping device ($\langle p|p^\prime\rangle=\delta(p-p^\prime)$).
Short questions: what is the spectrum of $H$ for a finite well, a free particle, the oscillator; why plane waves are not states.

enc.title: Old quantum theory: Planck and Bohr-Sommerfeld

blocks.html: Planck (1900). Classically each mode of cavity radiation carries $k_BT$ (Rayleigh-Jeans), and the energy density diverges at high frequency. Planck: a mode of frequency $ u$ exchanges energy only in quanta $h u$. The mean energy per mode is then $ rac{h u}{e^{h u/k_BT}-1}$:
Bohr-Sommerfeld (1915). Allowed classical orbits of a bound one-dimensional system are those with quantised action:

Oscillator: the orbit $\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac12m\omega_0^2q^2=E$ is an ellipse with semi-axes $\sqrt{2mE}$ and $\sqrt{2E/m\omega_0^2}$, area $\pi\sqrt{2mE}\sqrt{2E/m}/\omega_0=2\pi E/\omega_0$, so $E_n=n\hbar\omega_0$ (1.19), matching Planck. The exact result $\hbar\omega_0(n+\frac12)$ needs the full theory (WKB adds the $\frac12$).
Phase space comes in cells of area $h$: the old quantum theory picks the orbits that enclose an integer number of cells.
Bohr-Sommerfeld misses the zero-point energy and fails for systems that are not separable; it is a semiclassical rule, not quantum mechanics.
Older short questions: derive $E_n$ of the oscillator or the Bohr radius from quantisation conditions; Rayleigh-Jeans as the $h\to0$ limit.

check.explain: Area of the ellipse $2\pi E/\omega_0=2\pi n\hbar$.
